title: Export controls can restrict the targeted trade while spilling into firms' other markets and payroll
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-50 using export transactions, product control classifications, and firm-level outcomes
geography: United States exporters, controlled products, Russia-related export restriction in 2014, firms, products, and destinations

observations.period: 2010-2024 export-control prevalence; 2014 Russia restriction natural experiment

denominator.unit: firm-product-destination export transaction and firm-outcome analysis

control_prevalence.value: the share of U.S. exports subject to controls doubled between 2010 and 2024

firm_distribution.value: firms exporting controlled products have a skewed size distribution

targeted_market.value: the 2014 restriction reduced affected firms' probability of exporting targeted goods to Russia

spillover_exports.value: affected firms also reduced exports of other products and to other destinations

interpretation.value: domestic costs of export controls extend beyond the directly restricted transactions

observations.method: The authors combine export transactions with product classifications used to administer controls and exploit the 2014 U.S. restriction on exports to Russia as a natural experiment for firm-level outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The abstract identifies firm-level export and payroll effects but does not establish the national welfare balance, security effectiveness, consumer incidence, worker layoffs, or whether firms later adapted through new products or destinations.
observations.subgroup: U.S. firms exporting controlled products, with skewed firm-size distribution; effects may differ by product, technology, destination, supply chain, ownership, worker composition, and preexisting market power.
observations.counterinterpretation: Export controls may achieve security, diplomatic, or technology-protection goals not captured by firm exports or payroll. Spillovers can reflect demand, sanctions, macroeconomic conditions, compliance costs, substitution, or strategic firm response; lower payroll is not identical to layoffs or household harm.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the export-transaction design, control classifications, 2014 Russia restriction, targeted and indirect export effects, and payroll outcome.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical restriction-to-domestic-firm-spillover pathway. It does not measure the policy's security success, diplomatic effect, national welfare, worker-level job loss, consumer prices, or durable firm adaptation.
